easy.heading: Waking Up My Brain With Some Simple Pips
easy.body:
Hey there! I hope you have your favorite drink ready because today's easy puzzle was such a treat. I started by scanning the grid for the biggest clues, and those greater than 5 constraints at (0,0) and (3,4) caught my eye immediately. Since the highest number on our dominoes is a 6, I knew those two spots had to be 6s. This gave me a great starting point for my first dominoes. I placed the [0,6] domino across (1,0) and (0,0), and used the [2,6] domino to fill (2,4) and (3,4).

From there, I looked at the middle of the board. There is an empty spot at (2,1), which meant I could place the [2,0] domino there to connect (2,2) and (2,1). The sum of 5 in the top right at (1,2) and (1,3) was the last piece of the puzzle for me. By using the [2,3] and [0,5] dominoes to satisfy the remaining sum of 6 and sum of 5 regions, everything just clicked into place. It felt so satisfying to see all those dots line up perfectly!

medium.heading: Getting Into The Groove With The Medium Grid
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today definitely stepped things up a notch, but it was still a lot of fun to untangle. I spent a little extra time looking at the empty cells at (0,2), (0,3), and (4,0). These are so helpful because they act like little walls that tell you exactly where a domino cannot go. I noticed the less than 2 constraint at (3,0) and paired it with the empty cell at (4,0) using the [0,2] domino. Since (3,0) had to be a 0 or a 1, and the domino was [0,2], it worked out perfectly.

The real breakthrough happened in the middle where we had that chain of equal cells at (2,0), (2,1), and (3,1). I had to find numbers that could satisfy those while also making sure (1,0) stayed greater than 4. I ended up using the [5,6] domino for (1,0) and (2,0), which made (2,0) a 6. That meant the other cells in that equal region also had to be 6s. Once I had those anchors, placing the [4,4] and [4,3] dominoes felt much more natural. It is all about finding that one common number that connects the different regions!

hard.heading: A Deep Dive Into Today's Big Challenge
hard.body:
Wow, Rodolfo Kurchan really gave us a workout with this hard puzzle! When I first saw that massive unequal region covering seven cells at the bottom, I will admit I had to take a big sip of coffee. I decided to start with the easiest win on the board: the sum of 6 constraint at (6,4). Since it is just a single cell, I knew it had to be a 6. I used the [3,6] domino to link (6,3) and (6,4), which gave me a solid corner to work from.

Next, I moved to the top left where we had four cells that all had to be equal. This was a perfect spot for my doubles. I used the [0,0] and [1,1] dominoes to fill that area, which really cleared out the board. The trickiest part was navigating the equal and sum regions in the middle without violating that big unequal zone. I had to be very careful with the [4,5], [1,5], and [2,6] dominoes. The breakthrough moment was realizing how the sum of 4 at (6,1) and (6,2) interacted with the equal constraint at (5,0) and (6,0). Once I figured out those were all 2s and 0s, the rest of the dominoes fell right into their slots.

explanation.tips: Always look for the constraints that only have one possible answer first, like a single-cell sum of 6 or a greater than 5 rule. These give you a starting point so you are not just guessing. Also, try to use your doubles in areas where multiple cells must be equal, as it is a quick way to satisfy those tricky regions.
explanation.learned: Today I learned that the unequal constraint is a fantastic way to narrow down which dominoes to use because it prevents you from using too many of the same number in one area. I also realized that looking at the empty cells first helps visualize the board's boundaries better, making it easier to see where the longer domino paths can actually fit.

faqs.question: How do you play the NYT Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: In Pips, you place a set of dominoes onto a grid so that every cell is covered. You must follow the rules in each colored region, such as making sure the numbers are equal, sum up to a certain total, or are greater or less than a specific number.

faqs.question: What does an empty cell mean in Pips?
faqs.answer: An empty cell in a Pips puzzle is a space that cannot be part of a domino. It acts as a permanent block on the grid, helping you figure out the orientation and placement of the dominoes around it.

faqs.question: Can dominoes be rotated in the Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Yes, dominoes can be placed either horizontally or vertically. Part of the challenge is figuring out which way each domino needs to face to satisfy the mathematical constraints of the regions it covers.

faqs.question: What is the unequal constraint in NYT Pips?
faqs.answer: The unequal constraint means that every number inside that specific colored region must be different. For example, if a region has three cells and an unequal rule, you cannot have two 4s in that region.

faqs.question: Are all dominoes used in every NYT Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Yes, each puzzle provides a specific list of dominoes that must all be placed on the grid. You use each domino from the list exactly once to complete the board.
